**Vignette: Malee, Age 52**

Malee grew up understanding that the sea was generous. She was born in a coastal province of Thailand, and the ocean shaped her childhood — the smell of salt air, the rhythm of fishing boats, the way the horizon seemed to promise something endless and good. By the time she was in her late thirties, she had built a quiet, ordered life. She had married a steady man named Somchai, raised two children, and found her way to work she genuinely loved as a librarian at a regional public library. She liked the hush of the stacks, the logic of the Dewey Decimal System, the feeling that knowledge could be organized and kept safe.

On the morning of December 26, 2004, she was visiting her mother's home near the coast when the tsunami struck. The water came without adequate warning — first the strange withdrawal of the sea, which she remembers thinking looked wrong in a way she couldn't name, and then the wall of it. She lost sight of her mother within seconds. She was pulled under, slammed against debris, and surfaced choking in water that was no longer water but a moving field of wreckage and bodies. She survived by clinging to a concrete pillar for what she believes was several hours. Her mother did not survive. Neither did her aunt or two neighbors she had known since childhood.

In the weeks and months that followed, Malee functioned in the way that people sometimes do after catastrophic loss — by moving. She helped with recovery efforts, arranged the funeral rites, returned to work. She told herself and others that she was coping. Somchai worried, but she reassured him. She did not speak about what she had seen in the water.

Now, nearly twenty years later, Malee sits across from her therapist and describes a life that has quietly narrowed around her. She has not returned to Thailand's coast. She avoids the news in monsoon season. At the library, she finds herself struggling to concentrate in ways that embarrass her — she will be re-shelving books and suddenly she is back in the water, the sound of it filling her ears, the cold pressure against her chest so real she has to grip the cart to stay standing. She calls these episodes "going away," and she has learned to hide them from her colleagues.

Sleep is its own ordeal. She wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, her heart hammering, the dream always some variation of the same thing — her mother's face disappearing beneath the surface, Malee reaching and reaching and never closing the distance. She gets up and makes tea and sits at the kitchen table until the light comes. Somchai has learned not to ask too many questions in those hours. She loves him for that, and feels guilty that she cannot give him more.

What troubles Malee most, she says, is how ordinary triggers undo her. Rain on the library's skylight. A patron who comes in soaking wet and shakes off an umbrella. A documentary playing on a patron's laptop that she glimpsed only for a moment — aerial footage of a flooded city — and which sent her into the staff bathroom for fifteen minutes, sitting on the floor breathing carefully. She is a woman who has spent her adult life helping people find information, helping children fall in love with stories, believing in the organizing power of language. And yet there are things inside her that she cannot file, cannot catalog, cannot make orderly or safe.

She describes herself as "not the person I was before." She says this matter-of-factly, without self-pity, which somehow makes it harder to hear. She is still devoted to her work, still present for her family. But she carries the water with her everywhere she goes, and she is very, very tired.
